Senses.Explanation: People described as unable to see, hear, and speak. In the Chan record, the full phrase becomes the stable wording of Xuansha Shibei's “three kinds of invalids” public case. Xuansha asks how one receives people who cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, hear spoken command, or answer. Yuanwu Keqin warns his audience against treating his discussion as nothing more than the disability list, then asks where the blind, deaf, and mute fellow stands; Xuedou Chongxian begins his verse with the same phrase. In a Yunmen case, Yunmen tests an unnamed monk for deafness and muteness, and Xuedou applies the full phrase to him. Yuelin Shiguan later labels and re-asks Xuansha's case. Senses.Explanation: Itinerant monks who travel between monasteries and are received, housed, counted, and fed by Chan communities. The compound occurs 789 times in 238 texts. Hongzhi Zhengjue directly tells an addressee, 'Cloud-and-water is you; you are cloud-and-water,' immediately after describing a patch-robed monk taking a staff and circling the world. Sanshan Denglai counts cloud-and-water monks in the two halls; Wuzhun Shifan's biography records hundreds of rooms built to receive them; Fushi Tongxian directs visitors to the cloud-and-water hall; and Jie Weizhou recalls their doubled numbers during famine and the provisions used to sustain them. At the end of retreat, Tianyin Yuanxiu describes groups leaving the mountains in threes and twos as cloud-and-water roaming onward. The expanded noun 'cloud-and-water monk' occurs 17 times in 14 texts, while reception and hall constructions show that the shorter compound can name the same people without an explicit word for monk.
